title: Reading an error message and a stack trace
summary: Turn a red wall of text into three facts: what went wrong, why, and on which line of your code.
youWillLearn: The three parts of every error: type, message and location
How to read a stack trace and find the first line that is your code
Why ?. can hide a bug instead of fixing it

glossary.browser: The program Maya uses to open websites, like Chrome or Safari. It shows Notely's screens and sends her clicks on.
glossary.app server: A computer that runs the app's own code and answers the browser. While you build, it runs on your laptop.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: Notely sends it a note, it sends a summary back.
glossary.terminal: A plain text window where you type commands and where a running program prints its messages.
glossary.error: A message the program produces when it cannot continue, telling you what went wrong and where.
glossary.TypeError: An error that means a value was used the wrong way, most often reading a field of something that is undefined.
glossary.undefined: JavaScript's word for 'there is no value here', for example a field that does not exist.
glossary.JSON: A plain text format apps use to send data to each other, made of names and values in curly braces.
glossary.stack trace: The list of function calls that were running when the error happened, most recent call at the top.
glossary.frame: One line of a stack trace: one function call, with its file, line and column.
glossary.node_modules: The folder where installed packages live. Code in it belongs to libraries and frameworks, not to you.
glossary.source map: A file that maps the compressed code a live site runs back to your original files and line numbers.
glossary.optional chaining: The ?. operator: it gives back undefined instead of crashing when the value before it is missing.

steps.title: Notely's Summarize button, on your laptop
body: Click Summarize in Notely, our notes app, and the browser (the screen you use) sends the note to the app server (the computer running Notely's code), which asks the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, for a summary.
For now it all runs on your laptop, and the app server prints messages in a terminal, a text window.

scene.caption: A click goes from the browser to the app server and on to the Claude API. The terminal shows what the server prints.

steps.title: The summary never comes back
body: You click Summarize to test it. Nothing appears. The terminal fills with red text, and the bug could be anywhere in Notely's 3,000 lines.
The reflex is to paste all of it into Claude Code and type "fix". But an error is not noise. Its first lines usually say what broke and where. Reading them takes thirty seconds.

callout.text: This module is about finding causes yourself. Not to replace Claude Code, but so you can tell it where to look and judge whether its fix is real.

changes: ~ App Server crashes and answers with an error
~ Terminal fills with red text
~ The error none → red wall
~ Lines to check 0 → 3,000

scene.caption: The app server crashes. The terminal fills with red text.

steps.title: Every error has three parts
body: Look only at the first two lines of the red text. Every error answers three questions. Type: what kind of mistake. Message: what happened, in one sentence. Location: the file, line and column.
Read them in that order. Most of the time you know the cause before you reach the end.

callout.text: A note on your door: "Parcel not delivered (type). Nobody answered the bell (message). 14 Elm St, side door (location)." You would not call the courier before reading it.

code.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')
    at summarize (app/api/summary/route.ts:14:32)
code.caption: Type, then message, then location: file route.ts, line 14, column 32.

changes: − Browser, App Server, Claude API, Terminal: we zoom in
+ Error: the first two lines of the red text
+ Type, Message, Location: the three parts it carries
~ The error red wall → TypeError

scene.caption: One error, split into the three answers it always carries.

steps.title: The type names the kind of mistake
body: A few types cover most bugs. TypeError: a value was used the wrong way, very often because it was undefined (empty). ReferenceError: a name that does not exist, like a typo. SyntaxError: text that cannot be read, like broken JSON (the text format apps send data in).
Ours is a TypeError. So something had no value.

callout.text: Unexpected token '<' ... is not valid JSON means your code expected data but received a web page, usually an error or login page. The real problem is the request, not the reading.

changes: ~ Type in focus: TypeError
~ Message and Location fade back for now

scene.caption: First stop: the type. It narrows the search before you read anything else.

steps.title: The message, read as a sentence
body: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0') means: the code asked for item [0], the first item, of something. And that something was undefined.
So the bug is not the [0]. It is whatever came right before it. The real question becomes: why was that value empty?
changes: ~ Message in focus: reading item 0 of nothing
~ Type fades back

scene.caption: The message points at the value before [0]. That value was empty.

steps.title: A stack trace is a trail of calls
body: The location is the top line of a stack trace: the chain of function calls that led to the crash. The diagram reads left to right, top line first.
Each line is one frame: a function, its file, line and column. Each was called by the next one. POST, the function that answers the browser's request, called summarize.

code.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')
    at summarize (app/api/summary/route.ts:14:32)
    at async POST (app/api/summary/route.ts:6:18)
    at async node_modules/next/dist/server/...
    at async node:internal/process/...
code.caption: Real paths often carry extra prefixes. The file name and line still match yours.

changes: − Error, Type, Message, Location: we read further down
+ summarize, POST: two functions in Notely's code
+ Next.js, Node.js: the tools that run Notely's code

scene.caption: The stack trace, top line on the left: where it broke, then who called it, back to where it started.

steps.title: Find the first line that is yours
body: Long traces are mostly framework code: installed tools such as Next.js, the toolkit Notely is written with. Skip every frame in node_modules or node:internal. The bug is almost never there.
Read from the top and stop at the first file you or Claude Code wrote. Here that is route.ts (Notely's Summarize code), line 14. Open it there.

callout.text: On a live site, browser traces can point at compressed files like chunk-8f2a.js:1:48213. A source map translates that back to your file and line. Error trackers such as Sentry use them.

changes: ~ Next.js and Node.js fade: not your code
~ summarize: the first frame in your own code
~ Lines to check 3,000 → 1

scene.caption: Framework frames fade. The top frame in your own code is where to start.

steps.title: Notely's bug, read line by line
body: Line 14 is data.content[0].text, so data.content was undefined. You print data with console.log and see why: the Claude API answered with status code 429, "too many requests". Error answers have no content.
The code never checked. The fix: check res.ok (true only for a successful answer) first, and throw an error that says what really happened.

code.caption: Now the terminal starts with "Claude API 429" instead of a puzzle about undefined.

callout.text: The 429 itself is a separate problem: Notely asked too often, too fast. Waiting and retrying is covered in the AI module. This lesson is about making the error say so.

changes: + Browser, App Server, Claude API, Terminal: back to Notely
− summarize, POST, Next.js, Node.js
~ The error TypeError → Claude 429: too many requests
~ App Server now checks the answer before reading it

scene.caption: The real cause sat one step earlier: an error answer from the Claude API.

steps.title: Optional chaining hides, it does not fix
body: Instead of checking res.ok, a common "fix" for the crash is data?.content?.[0]?.text. Optional chaining (?.) stops the crash. It also turns a loud, readable error into a silent blank summary.
You, and later Maya, see an empty box, the terminal shows nothing, and the 429 is still there. Use ?. only when a missing value is truly normal.

callout.text: When Claude Code says "fixed", ask: which line of the trace was it, and why was the value undefined? Search its diff for new ?., || "" and empty catch {}. Each may hide the error instead of removing its cause.

changes: ~ App Server: ?. instead of the res.ok check
~ Browser shows a blank box; Terminal goes quiet
~ The error Claude 429 → hidden
~ Lines to check 1 → 3,000: the clue is gone

scene.caption: With ?. everywhere, nothing crashes, the page shows a blank box, and the terminal is silent.

steps.title: Recap: thirty seconds of reading
body: Read the type, then the message as a plain sentence, then the location. In the stack trace, skip framework frames and open the first line of your own code.
Then ask why the value was wrong, one step earlier. Fix that cause, and keep errors loud enough to read next time.
changes: ~ App Server: ?. removed, res.ok check back
~ Browser and Terminal back to normal
~ The error hidden → Claude 429, loud and clear
~ Lines to check 3,000 → 1

scene.caption: A loud, specific error points straight at the real cause.

quiz.question: Notely crashes with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title') on the line note.title. What does that tell you?

options.text: The title column is missing from the notes table.
options.why: A missing column would make note.title undefined, not crash. The crash means note itself was undefined.

options.text: note was undefined, so ask why no note was found or passed in.
options.why: "Reading 'title'" names the field being read. The thing it was read from, note, had no value. The cause is wherever note should have been set.

options.text: There is a typo in the word title.
options.why: A typo in a field name gives undefined quietly. A typo in a variable name gives a ReferenceError, not this TypeError.

quiz.question: A stack trace has 25 lines. The top three are in node_modules/next, line four is app/notes/[id]/page.tsx:22:9. Where do you start?

options.text: The very first line, since that is where the error was thrown.
options.why: It was thrown there, but inside framework code that is almost never wrong. It is usually reacting to a bad value your code passed in.

options.text: The last line, since that is where everything started.
options.why: The bottom is the start of the request, often deep in Node.js internals. It rarely says anything about your bug.

options.text: page.tsx, line 22: the first frame that is your code.
options.why: The first frame in your own files is where your code handed the framework something it could not handle. Open the file at that line.

quiz.question: Claude Code "fixes" a crash by changing user.profile.name to user?.profile?.name ?? "". The crash is gone. What should you ask next?

options.text: Why was user or profile missing, and is that ever normal?
options.why: Optional chaining removes the symptom. If a missing profile is a real bug, the page now shows a blank name and nobody notices.

options.text: Nothing. No crash means the bug is fixed.
options.why: A silent wrong result is often worse than a crash, because no log or error will tell you about it later.

options.text: Ask it to wrap the whole page in try/catch as well.
options.why: That hides even more errors. You want errors to be loud and specific, then fix their cause.

takeaways: Every error has a type, a message and a location. Read all three before you ask anyone for help.
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x') means the thing before .x had no value. Find out why.
In a stack trace, skip node_modules and internals. Start at the first line of your own code.
Check res.ok before reading an API answer, and throw errors that say what really happened.
Be suspicious of fixes made of ?., || "" and empty catch blocks: they hide errors.
